title: Pravda Replikanta — Curious Minds Edition
lead: How a humanoid switches between motions, and why completing a task is not the whole story.

news.title: FORGE gives Unitree G1 several ways to move
news.summary: A two-stage method connects forward motion, side steps, turns and hopping.
news.details: A simplified physical model generates movement references, and a whole-body controller follows them.
news.technical_novelty: Feasible reference generation is separated from detailed execution.
news.engineering_impact: A shared framework could ease transitions between locomotion modes.
news.limitations: The authors report forward speeds up to 2.8 m/s, lateral speeds of ±1.0 m/s and turning up to ±3.0 rad/s; all-terrain reliability is unproven.
news.evidence_status: Research preprint with author-run Unitree G1 demonstrations; no independent replication reported.
news.body:
Why is it hard for a humanoid to walk quickly, turn and hop using the same system? Each movement places different demands on balance. FORGE first calculates a motion with a simplified model, then has the robot's whole-body controller execute it.

On Unitree G1, the researchers report forward motion up to 2.8 m/s, sideways motion up to ±1.0 m/s, turning up to ±3.0 rad/s, and one-legged hops. It is a compelling unified demonstration, not a promise that the robot can handle any surface or unexpected obstacle.

news.title: QCP asks whether a task was done well, not merely completed
news.summary: A robot policy can take speed, smoothness and stability as explicit quality goals.
news.details: Successful runs are measured, relabeled and reused for further training.
news.technical_novelty: Execution quality becomes a condition on action selection.
news.engineering_impact: A conveyor rewards speed, while carrying wine glasses rewards stable movement.
news.limitations: The authors report improvements on RoboMimic and RoboEval plus real conveyor and glass-carrying tests, without a universal effect size.
news.evidence_status: Research preprint with author-run experiments; independent industrial validation is not reported.
news.body:
Imagine two robots carrying a glass. Both arrive, but one moves smoothly while the other almost spills its contents. A simple success-or-failure score treats them alike. QCP instead lets the robot policy take movement quality as a goal.

The system measures successful attempts and uses their quality labels for further learning. Researchers tested it on benchmarks and physical tasks, including a conveyor and wine glasses. The next question is whether the gains persist with different robots and objects.

technology_signal.title: Robots must control how they act, not only what they do
technology_signal.summary: FORGE connects locomotion modes; QCP makes execution quality adjustable.
technology_signal.implications: Both are research results, not evidence of universal capabilities.
